opus-5.5.text:
I think both are necessary, and they're actually complementary rather than competing.

Scenario-led startups start from a concrete problem, like a specific step in a factory line, a warehouse picking task, or cleaning in commercial buildings. Their advantage is that they get close to real customers very quickly. They learn what "good enough" means in practice: what success rate a customer will pay for, what cycle time matters, how often a human has to step in. That kind of knowledge is extremely valuable and very hard to get in a lab. The risk is that they end up building a lot of custom engineering for each deployment. Then it becomes more like a system integration business, and it's hard to scale or carry what they've learned into the next scenario.

Technology-led startups working on foundation models take the opposite bet. They believe that if you can build a general model, one that understands vision, language, and action across many embodiments and tasks, the marginal cost of each new application will drop dramatically. That's the path that could eventually unlock truly general-purpose robots. But the challenge is data and grounding. Robotics doesn't have an internet-scale dataset lying around, and a model that looks impressive in demos can still fall apart on the long tail of real-world conditions. If you're too far from real deployments, you can optimize for the wrong things.

So in my view, the healthiest ecosystem is one where these two kinds of companies feed each other. Foundation model teams provide stronger and stronger base capabilities. Scenario-led teams take those capabilities into the field and generate real-world data and feedback, which shows where the models fail. Over time, I expect the boundary to blur. The best scenario companies will build their own learning-based stacks, and the best foundation model companies will need to pick a few beachhead scenarios to prove value and close the data loop.

If I had to give advice to founders, it would be this: whichever side you start from, you need a clear story for how you get to the other side. A scenario company needs a path to generalization, and a model company needs a path to real deployment. Otherwise you're either stuck doing projects or stuck doing demos.

r001.rationale: It describes complementary scenario-led and foundation-model startups, but does not say that developing both hardware and foundation models within one company demands large resources or that this motivates dividing the work among specialized teams.

r002.rationale: It says the two kinds of companies can feed each other through capabilities, deployment data, and feedback, but does not argue that specialized robotics teams need collaboration or resource sharing to remain commercially sustainable.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the two kinds of companies are actually solving different problems, and the mistake people make is treating them as competitors on the same track.

Scenario-led startups start from a concrete problem: a warehouse that can't hire enough pickers, a kitchen that needs to turn out the same dish ten thousand times, a hospital that needs things moved between floors at night. Their advantage is that they touch reality every single day. They know what the failure modes look like, what the customer will actually pay for, and what "good enough" means in that environment. Their data is messy but it's real, and that matters enormously, because a lot of what breaks robotics isn't the model, it's the long tail of the physical world. Dust, lighting, a box that's slightly crushed, a person stepping into the path. You only learn those by being there.

The weakness is that the scenario can become a ceiling. You build a very good system for one setting, and then every new setting feels like starting over. Margins can be thin because you're also carrying hardware, deployment, and support.

Technology-led startups building foundation models are betting on the opposite thing: that generalization will come, and that whoever owns the general capability owns the leverage. If that bet pays off, they become something like the operating system layer, and the scenario companies become applications on top. That's a very attractive position. But right now it's still a bet. Robot data is scarce compared to text, it's expensive to collect, and a model that looks impressive in a demo can still fall apart in a real deployment. So these companies carry a different risk: they can spend years and a lot of capital before anyone pays for the output.

What I actually think is that the healthy outcome is a loop between the two. The scenario companies generate the hard, grounded data and the honest feedback about what fails. The model companies turn that into capabilities that make the next deployment cheaper and faster. Over time, I expect the best companies to have a bit of both inside them. A scenario company that doesn't invest in learning-based generalization will get commoditized, and a model company that never goes to a real site will keep training on the wrong distribution.

So if I'm advising founders, I'd say: pick the one that matches your team's DNA and your honest assessment of the timeline, but don't pretend the other half doesn't exist. If you're scenario-led, build your data and your software architecture so you can ride the wave when general models arrive. If you're model-led, get a real customer early, even if it's unglamorous, because that contact with reality is what separates a paper from a product.

r001.rationale: The response describes different risks for scenario-led and model-led startups, but does not say that developing robotics hardware and foundation models within one company demands too many resources or that this is why the work should be divided among specialized teams.

r002.rationale: The response advocates a feedback loop between scenario and model companies, but does not argue that specialized teams need collaboration or resource sharing to sustain their work commercially.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re starting from two different ends of the same problem. A scenario-led startup starts with a customer need: what task needs to be done, in what environment, and at what cost? Then it works backward to the technology. A technology-led startup starts with a capability, like a robotics foundation model, and asks how broadly that capability can be applied.

The advantage of being scenario-led is that you have a concrete feedback loop. You can deploy, discover what fails, collect relevant data, and measure whether you’re creating value. The risk is that every deployment becomes a custom engineering project. You might build a useful business without developing something that scales across tasks.

For a foundation-model company, the opportunity is to create capabilities that many applications can share. But you still need real-world deployments to test whether that generality is useful. A compelling demo doesn’t necessarily tell you whether a robot can perform reliably enough for a customer to pay for it.

So I see these approaches as complementary. Application companies can provide the deployment experience and feedback that model companies need, while better models can reduce the engineering required for each application. The interesting question is where that relationship settles: how much can the model provide out of the box, and how much value still comes from understanding a particular customer’s workflow?

r001.rationale: The response contrasts scenario-led and technology-led startups but does not identify the resource demands of developing robotics hardware and foundation models within one company or recommend dividing that work among specialized teams.

r002.rationale: It describes complementary feedback and model benefits, but does not argue that specialized robotics teams need collaboration or resource sharing to remain commercially viable.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as two different starting points that can eventually converge. A scenario-led company starts with a specific customer problem: what task needs to be done, in what environment, and at what cost? It can build a tight feedback loop between deployment, data collection, and product improvement. The challenge is making sure the solution can scale beyond one customer or one narrowly defined task.

A technology-led company starts with the belief that a more general model will unlock many applications. That can create much broader possibilities, but it still needs real-world deployment to understand where the technology works, where it fails, and what customers will pay for.

So I wouldn’t say one approach is inherently better. The key question is whether you can connect technical progress with a useful product. Scenario-led companies need a path toward greater generality, and foundation-model companies need a path toward concrete customer value. There’s also room for them to work together rather than each trying to build the entire stack.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes scenario-led and technology-led companies as different starting points that may converge, but does not identify the resource demands of building robotics hardware and foundation models in one company as a reason to divide the work.

r002.rationale: It says the two types of companies could work together, but does not argue that specialized robotics teams need collaboration or resource sharing to remain commercially viable.
